title: Tendai
hookLine: the Japanese form of Tiantai on Mount Hiei, home of many founders

cards: Dogen. Nichiren. Say those names to someone who knows Japanese Buddhism and they'll hear founders: the Pure Land schools, Zen lines, the Nichiren schools.
Teachers who went in different directions and sometimes argued hard. Now ask where each of them began.
Tradition gives the same answer again and again: a forested mountain above Kyoto, where they studied as young monks before they ever founded anything. One slope, many roads leading down from it.

teach.b: A Japanese monk named Saicho traveled to China, studied the Tiantai teaching, and brought it home to Mount Hiei; in Japanese the name is said Tendai. This path met Saicho and his mountain before.
Today's question is a different one: what did the school hold, that so many roads could come out of it? Tendai kept the Lotus Sutra at its center, as Tiantai did.
But on Mount Hiei the monks also trained in meditation, kept the monastic precepts, practiced esoteric ritual with mantras and mandalas, and chanted the name of Amida Buddha.
All under one roof: less a single practice than a whole curriculum, a rope of many strands.
Later teachers who trained there each, in his own way, took hold of one strand and found the whole rope in it. Honen and Shinran took the calling of Amida's name.
Eisai and Dogen took meditation, and brought Zen lineages back from China. Nichiren took the Lotus Sutra itself. Their schools have their own stories, and the path will reach them soon.
Tradition calls Mount Hiei the mother mountain of Japanese Buddhism.
A mother isn't the same as her children, and children don't always agree with their mother, or with each other; some of these founders left the mountain in sharp disagreement.
But the name holds something true: they learned to read, chant and sit in the same place. And Tendai didn't vanish when its children left.
It is still practiced on the mountain today, holding many strands at once.

how: Tendai Buddhists in Japan study the Lotus Sutra and combine meditation, precepts, esoteric ritual and recitation of Amida Buddha's name; Mount Hiei remains the school's center of training.

games.q: you're a young monk on Mount Hiei, trained in many practices. one strand grips you more than the rest. what do the founders in today's story do?
o: take hold of one strand and make it the whole rope.
games.why: each later founder took one strand, Amida's name, meditation or the Lotus itself, and built a school around it.

practice: Bring to mind a place that taught you before you went your own way, a school, a kitchen, a first job, a team, a congregation, a family, whether you left it gladly or arguing.
Let one thing it gave you come up, a habit, a skill, a way of standing, and hold it for a few breaths. If you'd like, bow your head slightly toward it, inside.

wordCard.voice: Tendai. The Japanese form of Tiantai, founded on Mount Hiei by Saicho, holding the Lotus, meditation, precepts, ritual and the calling of Amida's name together. Today's word.

orig.note: the same characters as Chinese Tiantai, read in Japanese as Tendai.
